page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: Isotherms are the curves obtained when the
pressure of a gas is plotted against its volume
steps.why: Iso means same and therm means temperature: one curve collects all the P–V states of the gas that share one temperature.
common_mistakes: Naming the wrong pair of axes. Isotherms are P against V.
Leaving out at constant temperature — that condition is the definition.
steps.memory_tip: Iso-therm: same temperature. The plotted pair is the other two variables, P and V.
steps.margin_note: Axes plus the constant quantity make the complete definition.

steps.label: The constant quantity and the law

lines.text: Isotherm: a P–V curve of a gas at constant temperature

lines: Each temperature gives its own curve; Boyle's law
(PV = constant) is the behaviour along one isotherm.
steps.why: Connecting the curve to Boyle's law shows what the curve says: along it PV stays constant, which is why an ideal-gas isotherm bends like a rectangular hyperbola.
common_mistakes: Attaching Charles' law here. Charles' law belongs to constant pressure, not constant temperature.
steps.memory_tip: Constant T goes with Boyle's law: PV = constant along every isotherm.
steps.margin_note: The Boyle's law link is the detail that separates a full answer from a bare definition.

insider_note: The three cousin terms — isotherm, isobar, isochore — are asked as a set; keeping the constant quantity straight for each is the whole task.
